body:
If `opposite` is meant to be true only when there's an uneven number of negative coordinates in the two vectors, you can use dot product to assess it:
```
	print(Vector2(-1, 1).dot(Vector2(1, 1)))
	print(Vector2(-1, -1).dot(Vector2(1, 1)))
	print(Vector2(1, -1).dot(Vector2(1, 1)))
	print(Vector2(1, -1).dot(Vector2(1, -1)))
	print(Vector2(1, -1).dot(Vector2(-1, -1)))
	print(Vector2(1, -1).dot(Vector2(-1, 1)))
```
prints:
```
0
-2
0
2
0
-2
```
When it's 0, it's `opposite` in your code.

I'm a bit rusty on my math but I'm sure there must be a geometric explanation for why this would be the "proper" way to compare the signedness of two unit vectors.
author: akien-mga

body:
> I'm a bit rusty on my math but I'm sure there must be a geometric explanation for why this would be the "proper" way to compare the signedness of two unit vectors.

Well basically it just means that the two unit vectors are orthogonal in the Cartesian space. If they were colinear, the signs would either be the same or opposite for both coordinates.

(Seems like I just had to call myself "rusty" to remember some math :P)

body: The code is good, but I have a small suggestion! Instead of checking if each key is pressed which can harm performance, why not check to see if any key was pressed using only 1 if statement! This can be easily done by creating an integer counter before the for loop and initialized to 0, then instead of doing `if (E->get().pressed)` we do `counter += (int)E->get().pressed` .. after the for loop, if the counter is over 0, then a key was pressed.
author: RebelliousX

body:
I just profiled both current and your suggestion, I couldn't detect much performance difference (at most 1 usec improvement). That's around going through 5-8 actions. With the counter, you do have to go through all actions. But when you detect if the action is pressed, you can just exit the loop with `return` immediately. Most of the time the user would actually be pressing something, so we're interested in short-cutting I think. If the user is away, the performance doesn't matter anyway. So, readability would be preferred in this case imo.

I'll try to see if there's any more significant difference with more actions, but I doubt the user would like to define many of them. In fact, it's not going through all `InputMap` actions, but only those which were pressed during gameplay. It means that the more actions you press, the more the `action_state` would look like an `InputMap`.

author: RandomShaper

body:
Maybe:
```
"Invalid operands for bit shifting. Only positive operands are supported, and the right hand side operand cannot be higher than 62."
```

That being said, I don't think if it's worth it to limit to `b <= 62`.
It will still wrap around if you do `2 << 62` with a signed int, or `4 << 62` with an unsigned it. Only `1 << 62` would be safe.

IMO a note in the documentation should be sufficient to make users aware that bitshifting can lead to wrapping around if they exceed the number of bits of the used type. Maybe we can have some GDScript warnings for that eventually too, but I wouldn't prevent the operation if we can't guarantee that we handle all cases.

So I'd suggest leaving it to only signessness checks, and the error:
```
Invalid operands for bit shifting. Only positive operands are supported.
```
author: akien-mga

body:
I think the message @akien-mga proposes is more accurate and user-friendly than the one in the PR.

The one in the PR says the reason for the error is undefined behavior, but that's too an obscure term for most users. In addition, the fact that it's UB in C++ doesn't necessarily mean that it has to be in GDScript. GDScript could implement a defined behavior, only that we won't and we just want not to support shifts with negatives involved.

The PR is fine to me besides that.

body:
Yes .. they don't result in the same behaviour! The old code was broken badly. #26637 

This was the original reason for the PR, the use of height (and the 2x multiplier) fixes the bug.

It turns out that when you pass size into CameraMatrix::set_orthogonal, size only persists in terms of the height dimension (unless the aspect ratio is 1.0). To get back to the original size in order to create a new CameraMatrix, you have to use the HEIGHT rather than the width. I.e. height is preserved rather than width. This makes sense for typical use cases of aspect ratio.

body:
The work overall looks really good, and it's going to be a great improvement.

Some things worries me though:

1. This will break workflow for people who uses different scripts for client and server. Unless the script have the same exposed RPC/RSET (order shouldn't matter since sorting is done based on case). This is okay in general, but it needs to fail properly. Maybe we can spend a byte to do a checksum (xors of function names/...) so it's detectable and we can report it.

2. As pointed out in comments, if I understood correctly the code, exposing a new method via rpc_config will just append it. This means that different rpc_config order will result in differnt ids being assigned, and the wrong function to be called. Shouldn't we re-sort them when that happens? That will fix that problem, but ongoing calls with that ID will fail instead. For now, `rpc_config` seems to crash the engine when the new RPC is sent (see attached code).

3. The encoding optimization should probably be moved to marshalls, but I guess that could be done in a later PR.

Of all the points, `2` worries me the most. I feel we have to find a solution to that. Do you have anything in mind (maybe some form of versioning?). Using an agreed upon ID like we do for paths is less optimized and it would be a pity to waste the work done so far on generating the ID.

The folling code crash the engine (rpc_config):
```gdscript
extends Node

func _ready():
	var args = Array(OS.get_cmdline_args())
	while args.size():
		var a = args.pop_front()
		if a == 'c':
			var peer = NetworkedMultiplayerENet.new()
			peer.create_client("localhost", 8092)
			multiplayer.connect("network_peer_connected", self, "_connected")
			multiplayer.connect("network_peer_packet", self, "_pkt")
			multiplayer.set_network_peer(peer)
		elif a == 's':
			var peer = NetworkedMultiplayerENet.new()
			peer.create_server(8092)
			multiplayer.connect("network_peer_connected", self, "_connected")
			multiplayer.connect("network_peer_packet", self, "_pkt")
			multiplayer.set_network_peer(peer)
	rpc_config("_added", MultiplayerAPI.RPC_MODE_REMOTESYNC)
	rpc_config("_other", MultiplayerAPI.RPC_MODE_REMOTESYNC)

func _pkt(p_id : int, pkt : PoolByteArray):
	if pkt[0] != 0:
		return # Just for testing
	if not multiplayer.is_network_server():
		prints(p_id, pkt.subarray(1, pkt.size() - 1).get_string_from_utf8(), "at", OS.get_ticks_msec())
		multiplayer.send_bytes(pkt, 1)
	else:
		pkt = pkt.subarray(1, pkt.size() - 1)
		print("Recv ping at: %s = %s" % [OS.get_ticks_msec(), OS.get_ticks_msec() - int(pkt.get_string_from_utf8())])
		return
		multiplayer.send_bytes(str(OS.get_ticks_msec()).to_utf8(), p_id)

func _connected(p_id):
	print("Connected to: %d" % p_id)
	if multiplayer.is_network_server():
		while true:
			yield(get_tree().create_timer(1),"timeout")
			if not p_id in multiplayer.get_network_connected_peers():
				break
			print("Sending ping at ", OS.get_ticks_msec())
			var pkt = PoolByteArray([0])
			pkt.append_array(str(OS.get_ticks_msec()).to_utf8())
			multiplayer.send_bytes(pkt, p_id)
			rpc_id(p_id, "_ping", OS.get_ticks_msec())
			rpc("_added", "Added Called") #### !!!!!!!!!!! CRASH HERE.
			rpc("_other", "Other Called")

	if multiplayer.is_network_server():
		var ticks = OS.get_ticks_msec()
		print("Ping: %d" % ticks)
		rpc_id(p_id, "_ping", ticks)
		for i in range(0, 10):
			yield(get_tree().create_timer(1),"timeout")
			ticks = OS.get_ticks_msec()
			print("Ping: %d" % ticks)
			rpc_id(p_id, "_ping", ticks)

remote func _ping(time):
	print("Ping: %d" % time)
	rpc_id(1, "_pong", time)

remote func _pong(time):
	print("Pong: %d - %d = %d" % [OS.get_ticks_msec(), time, OS.get_ticks_msec() - time])

func _added(msg):
	print("Added called with: ", msg)
	pass
func _other(msg):
	print("Other called with: ", msg)
	pass
```

Reminder for self: Double check int/size comparisons.

body: I'm happy to make this change, but can you explain what the difference is? What makes `memdelete` a better choice than `memfree` in this instance? I'm pretty new to C++, so the answer might be really simple.
author: niklashigi

body:
In C++, memory allocated with `new` must be freed with `delete` and memory allocated with `alloc` must use `free`. Depending on the implementation `new` and `alloc` can track allocated memory separately (https://isocpp.org/wiki/faq/freestore-mgmt#mixing-malloc-and-delete), and `free` won't call object destructor.

With current Godot memory management implementation and no destructor in the `screensaver`, `memfree` might work, but it is wrong anyway.

body: There's an issue with this approach (drawing highlights for each glyph individually) if you are using font/script with the overlapping glyphs. On the screenshot, semi transparent `bgcolor` is covering part of the text. For this reason, text selection is fully drawn before drawing any text(see lines 940-953), same should be done for highlights: 1. Draw selection and `bgcolor` rectangles. 2. Draw text outlines. 3. Draw main text. 4. Draw `fgcolor` rectangles. Text server have dedicated for this specific purpose, which return non overlapping highlight/selection ranges for the portion of text: ``` Vector range = TS->shaped_text_get_selection(rid, start_position, end_position); ```

body:
I am against delta ever being allowed to be zero or negative.

Everyone expects delta to be change-in-time-since-last-process. It is physically impossible for a perfectly accurate timer to say no time has passed, as calling functions **always** takes time. If there is zero time between calls where things are time based, there's no point in calling it at all, so literally not calling _process if delta <= 0 is probably better.

Furthermore, if you divide by delta anywhere, you'll get bit, but it will be at a random time and likely not found until after release, assuming the development rig is sufficiently stout. This is not obvious at all and could be the source of major frustration for users who don't understand, and at worst, a slight financial loss requiring a software patch to be released.
author: Jimmio92

body:
> Everyone expects delta to be change-in-time-since-last-process. It is physically impossible for a perfectly accurate timer to say no time has passed, as calling functions always takes time

It is physically impossible to store a delta time less than the float epsilon, and I would vote in favor of more accurate long-term timers. If you add `delta` to a time variable every frame, and the script is executing faster than `1/epsilon` frames per second, then the timer would run too fast. Regardless, one would need hundreds of thousands of FPS to get a zero delta in the first place (possibly millions).
author: nathanfranke

body: For the timers Godot uses, granularity is bigger than the CPU clock (I think it was 10^6 ticks per second?). So yes, it is physically possible to get a measurement of zero for the passed time since the last frame, however improbable that is. If you're dividing by the delta argument to update, you're making two mistakes: Doing a potentially failing operation without checking, and doing a numerically unstable operation for small delta arguments. Yes, that these error sources exist is a surprise for novices. Ideally, we'd throw a delta=0 and delta=10^-6 argument at them in debug mode every once in a while to make everyone get used to the possibility; it's hard do so that without disrupting game flow, however.
author: zmanuel

body:
I don't see what all the fuss is. No gain will come from receiving a time based event with no time having passed. I for one cannot believe that this simple thing is so debated and left this way.

I have written toy engines myself in C and GL and have had to fix jitter and the like, and none of it was ever because no time passed between frames. This sounds 100% like covering up the real problem: Bad time source.

On Win32, QueryPerformanceCounter provides for nanosecond accuracy on most hardware that I tested. This guarantees that the second query will be after the first, and there's no way that, given the amount of work Godot must do, for a delta of 0 or less to EVER appear. Delta is simply current_frame_time - last_frame_time. If there's jitter, keep 7 of the last deltas, sort them, toss 0 and 6, 1,2,3,4,5 average, and give that value to process functions. I don't get why there's anything more needed.

Even if a zero time did appear, you're doing work based on time. Whatever that work is, you'd do none of it if delta was zero. Wasted cycles, wasted energy. Just throw out the process event if <= 0, seriously. It's not like anything is going to break... no time passed, remember? And the next tiny slice of time will get the process call, so again... no problems, but it's fixed. No potential gachas for newbies who (imo correctly) assume that time always marches forward. No chance of causing any issues because of a dropped _process, because it'll happen again *extremely* soon.

If I'm missing some key piece to this that would make this a no-go, please do clue me in.
author: Jimmio92

body:
You are 100% correct: All of this IS a way to compensate for a bad timer source. The problem isn't the timer resolution, though, it's that the time is taken on the CPU. In the best case (single threaded operation), when all the commands have been passed to the GPU. In the worst case (multithread), when all the scene data has been passed to the rendering thread. If you want stable frame time measurements, you should take the time when the GPU is starting to deliver the newly rendered frame to the screen. Alas, in GLES, that seems to be impossible. In Desktop OpenGL and Vulkan, you can use fences and queries to determine when the GPU flipped the buffers N frames ago. It's a bit difficult because it's asynchronous, but doable. Patches probably welcome.

The entire purpose of the file that is getting patched here is to take the imperfect timer measurements and derive stable process calls. Focus is on getting consistent number of physics steps per render frame. Without the code in this file, Godot would sometimes, even in perfect 60FPS VSync locked conditions, do jittery updates where each frame, anything between 0 and 2 physics updates were performed, because the imperfect timer measurements would lie just a little bit on either side of a threshold. Averaging over N frames makes these occurrences rarer, but does not fix them.

The negative timesteps that are corrected in this patch aren't coming from the timer itself, they're a bad output of the correction. Essentially, it's overshooting a bit one frame, then tries to backpedal. Maybe it would be possible to just prevent the overshooting; I don't think so, because that's what the system has to do to function correctly when frame times decrease. I opted for the post-correction also because that guarantees there are no side effects, it's easier to prove that the result will be correct, and it'll stay correct even if the core gets changed.

Just not calling _process() if the argument would be 0 is also not such a good option. There are three possible expectations here:
1. The sum of delta arguments to _process() is as close to the total program runtime as possible. Networked games rely on that.
2. the argument to _process() should be positive. That is what you want, even though it was never really guaranteed (just extremely unlikely to be false).
3. _process is called for every rendered frame. That is [documented](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/getting_started/step_by_step/scripting_continued.html?highlight=_process#processing).
Best possible conformance with expectation 1, in the situation covered here, requires to either violate 2 or 3. You get screamed at by someone no matter what :)

The current, updated patch opts to violate expectation 1 a little to save 2 and 3. But not more than it is allowed to; the limit on real time/game time deviation still is less than physics_jitter_fix/physics_fps. I personally would prefer to break bad client code, but do so early; I don't really see a way to do that well, though, and don't want that to be the hill this bugfix dies on.

It looks like there's a consensus that we should continue supporting multiple clients. The TCP_Server and StreamPeerTCP objects that we're already using will make this easy.
In general, what we need to change is:
Use a container of `peer`s instead of a single peer
When polling:

-  Add new peers to the container
- Iterate over each peer, removing dead/disconnected peers from the container and calling `on_data_received` for each peer

Most of the existing functions should be modified to accept a peer as a parameter, so they know which one they're working with (instead of using the global peer object we have now)

body:
@Shatur95 The reason we only plan on allowing a subset of modern C++ is to ease online code reviews (among other things). When you're a pull request reviewer, you typically don't clone people's branches in an IDE; you just rely on GitHub's code viewer which doesn't provide things like type information on hover. For instance, this is why we'll disallow the use of `auto` in Godot's codebase.

Unlike `auto`, `constexpr` doesn't suffer from readability issues, but I remember seeing reduz being opposed to it (I don't know why).

`constexpr` as for me is always better than macro constant because it do the same but in safe way.

body: I think all core types should be aligned to 8 bytes via attributes. Doing that is a bit different on all compilers, but I think it's clearer than this.
author: karroffel

body: Do you mean updating core types in Godot itself? Variant actually already had this attribute, but only for GCC. Do you suggest ensuring that Variant is 24 bytes on all platforms instead of this fix?
author: endragor

body:
No, I meant that at the moment none of the GDNative wrapper types have alignment specified and are represented as byte arrays, so their alignment is always `1`.

On x64 this is not much of a problem, but unaligned reads can be fatal on other platforms. Instead of converting the size to `int64_t[2] + int` I would keep the byte array but add explicit alignment.

The size still needs to be determined properly, of course, maybe the most clear way is actually to have just a bunch of `#if PLATFORM_X` to specify the size directly.
author: karroffel

body:
The alignment is `1` only if you specify that the struct is packed (which is another attribute). Otherwise compilers make them aligned by default, depending on the target platform. I'm still not sure why we should mess with alignment in these wrapper types. Their sole purpose is to have size equal to the types from Godot. So as long as it is fulfilled, I don't think we should add more complexity to their definitions.

Static checks added in this commit ensure that the sizes are equal on any platform Godot is compiled for.
author: endragor

body:
As far as I know, the alignment is always the biggest alignment of all the members. In this case all members are just `uint8_t`, so the alignment is always `1`. There is no way the compiler knows that the C wrapper types need to fit data that contains pointers or multi-byte integers.

https://godbolt.org/z/q7M4Gg

Additionally to size checks that you added we should also add alignment checks. In the GDNative C wrappers pointers to the C types are often just casted to pointers of the C++ type. Unaligned access can be a problem, even if the size matches.
author: karroffel

body:
The change makes the largest member int64_t which ensures 8-byte alignment. I don't understand why you insist on adding platform- or compiler- specific ifdefs, it would look more messy to me.

Alignment checks isn't a static thing. If allocator provides aligned addresses and the data itself is aligned (size is divisble by the required alignment), you'll have aligned pointers.
author: endragor

body: My apologies, I've now realized what you meant by alignment checks and agree they should be added. Still not sure about the ifdefs.
author: endragor

body:
I have no strong feelings about the `ifdef`s, I just think a solution that is clear and works on all architectures would be good.

The `sizeof(void *) + N` or hardcoded values can work, but it's less clear to read for me personally than a list of exceptions for example.

But I think we can deal with the size somehow. The mismatch of alignment however is something that keeps me awake at night :sweat_smile:

They actually should be debug only, I've wrapped them in #ifdef DEBUG_ENABLED. It is a check on program flow, if this assertion is violated the rest of the function won't work. body:
The PR looks good to me, although I'm a bit skeptic about the need for this feature.
Something similar can be achieved by using a regular `rpc` with a single PoolByteArray at the extra cost of 5 bytes but without using a new keyword and this extra logic.

That said, 5 bytes is not so little in the world of UDP, accounting to ~1% of safely usable payload and potentially increasing the network bandwidth of more than 1 KiB/s with just 4 such RPCs in process.

So, if others agree on the need of this feature, it's fine by me, and the code looks good.

body:
This is more of a quality of life improvement. 
Say you have two unsaved scenes open (_tab1*_, _tab2*_) and you're focused on the tab to the right (_tab2*_). When you exit the editor, the popup asks you if you want to save. Since Godot scans the unsaved scenes from left to right, the popup will ask what you want to do with _tab1*_, but it's still focused on _tab2*_. You save/discard, _tab1_ gets closed and then reopened by this fix, but it's appended on the right. So now you have _tab2*_ and _tab1_, popup asks for _tab2*_ but the editor is focused on _tab1_.
These lines make the editor focus on the tab the popup is asking you what to do with, otherwise Godot will always focus on the latest one to the right, so the user can't really see the tab Godot is asking him to do something with, and it's impossible to select it when the popup is present.
I thought it's better to let the user see the tab, so that he can better see if it's to be saved or not.
Actually, I checked the code and it's pointless to call `_update_scene_tabs()`, because it will get called anyway if necessary, but `_scene_tab_changed` has to be called to fix the issue I've just explained.

If this gets accepted anyway, this wont work. The number of frames per second in a game might vary, so this computation is definitely not going to output a correct duration if the FPS fluctuate. The timestamp of the action state change should be stored instead to compute the duration.

body:
Currently the `Engine` singleton provides the following methods related to FPS:
```cpp
Engine::get_iterations_per_second()
Engine::get_frames_per_second()
// Engine::get_target_fps()
```
From my understanding, `Engine::get_iterations_per_second()` returns the fixed/physics FPS.
If you look below, the idle frame timestamp is used in conjunction with `Engine::get_frames_per_second()` which can fluctuate as you say.

So if we take the fixed FPS, this should output the right duration, am I right?

If we take the idle FPS, then it should compute "the average" time instead? If that's the case then it should be documented then, because in most cases we're interested in fixed process for logic. That's why I linked #26828 because the engine already seem to have this kind of an issue in the first place.

> The timestamp of the action state change should be stored instead to compute the duration.

The engine already does it, unless you say about exposing the timestamp to script.

Doing this via script won't help either even with `get_toggle_timestamp()` added because the user will still try to implement similar logic for computing duration as in here.

Right, while reading if I though of the GDScript `match` statement where the default case is a catch-all, and cases are processed sequentially. But here indeed default is only used in absence of match.

`get_speaker_mode()` returns an enum value and all 4 possible values of the enum are handled, so I don't think we need to worry about potential uninitialization. If a 5th enum value was added, compilers would throw a warning (treated as error on CI) if it's not handled in the switch.

Great job! I love the attention to detail and the deep-fullsome explanations.

Most of the notes I left are about removing references to how the engine uses the resources internally. 

Keep in mind that these resources map onto Vulkan resources. What the engine uses is the Vulkan resources and not these ones directly. These are provided for the convenience of users so that they can create the underlying resource (e.g. CubemapArray) from images without having to access the Vulkan API directly. The engine just access the Vulkan API directly.

```suggestion
		[CubemapArray]s are made of an array of [Cubemaps]. Accordingly, like [Cubemap]s they are made of multiple textures the amount of which must be divisible by 6 (one image for each face of the cube). The primary benefit of [CubemapArray]s is that they can be accessed in shader code using a single texture reference. In other words, you can pass multiple [Cubemap]s into a shader using a single [CubemapArray].
		Generally, [CubemapArray]s provide a more efficent way for storing multiple [Cubemap]s, than storing multiple [Cubemap]s themselves in an array.
		Internally Godot, uses [CubemapArray]s for many effects including the [Sky], if you set [member ProjectSettings.rendering/reflections/sky_reflections/texture_array_reflections] to [code]true[/code].
		[b]Note:[/b] [CubemapArray] is not supported in the OpenGL 3 rendering backend.
```

Remember, the class reference documentation is intended for users who will be using these classes in their games. Notes about internal usage are not helpful for users as they will not be interacting with the underlying Graphics API directly. Class ref documentation needs to tell users why to use a given class, what that class does for them, and then warn them about usage (like how they aren't support in the OpenGL 3 backend).

It may be for CPU detection and dynamic dispatch in the third party code. MSVC allows you to explicitly use e.g. intrinsics above the architecture specified in the cl.exe command line, whereas gcc (and probably clang) do not afaik. body:
The relevant logic is in `dsp/dsp.h`:
```
#if defined(__SSE2__) || defined(WEBP_MSC_SSE2) || defined(WEBP_HAVE_SSE2)
#define WEBP_USE_SSE2
#endif

#if defined(__SSE4_1__) || defined(WEBP_MSC_SSE41) || defined(WEBP_HAVE_SSE41)
#define WEBP_USE_SSE41
#endif
```

I assume you're having this issue when using Clang with MSVC?
libwebp is written with the assumption that MSVC means that it can do what @lawnjelly described in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/36580#discussion_r385167821, but evidently that's not possible when using Clang instead of MS VC++.

Should we be prioritizing virtual GPUs over discrete GPUs? I'm not sure when deviceType would ever be ``VK_PHYSICAL_DEVICE_TYPE_VIRTUAL_GPU``, so I don't know what is best here. 

I feel like my above comment applies. Where a user has a discrete GPU it should be prioritized for now. Later we can add a command line argument to specify a particular GPU if users want to test software/emulated GPUs.

Another option is to make an enum and list them in priority order. e.g.
```
enum DeviceType {
VK_PHYSICAL_DEVICE_TYPE_OTHER, 
VK_PHYSICAL_DEVICE_TYPE_CPU, 
VK_PHYSICAL_DEVICE_TYPE_VIRTUAL_GPU, 
VK_PHYSICAL_DEVICE_TYPE_INTEGRATED_GPU, 
VK_PHYSICAL_DEVICE_TYPE_DISCRETE_GPU,
VK_PHYSICAL_DEVICE_TYPE_MAX
}
```
And then use that for your comparison to properly prioritize discrete GPUs

body:
Here's a script which could be used to help replace all occurrences (it's pretty naive and makes mistakes which need to be reviewed manually, and also needs to be run several times as it only handles the first occurrence in each file):
```bash
#!/bin/bash

files=$(rg -l memdelete)

for file in ${files}; do
  match=$(pcregrep -M 'memdelete\(([^\)]*)\);.*\n.*\1 = (NULL|nullptr|0)' "${file}" | cut -d $'\n' -f1)
  if [ ! -z "${match}" ]; then
    sed -i "/${match}/{n;d}" "${file}"
  fi
done
```

But @reduz says this wouldn't be a good idea anyway:
```
13:13 <reduz> Akien: it does not always have write access to the pointer
13:13 <reduz> Akien: and its kind of misleading
```

Might be good to specify what is the impact of using `immediate`.
I looked into the rendering code and `!p_immediate` is passed to:
```
Error RenderingDeviceVulkan::texture_update(RID p_texture, uint32_t p_layer, const Vector<uint8_t> &p_data, bool p_sync_with_draw) {
```
so "immediate" means `!p_sync_with_draw`, which is then used here:
```
        VkCommandBuffer command_buffer = p_sync_with_draw ? frames[frame].draw_command_buffer : frames[frame].setup_command_buffer;
```
Not sure what it means, gut feeling would be that "immediate" means force redrawing, while not immediate would mean that it redraws normally at the next schedule draw call. But I don't understand that easily from the code, so needs checking with @reduz or @clayjohn.

body:
I don't know about gradle integration specifically, but `release_debug` is the build type we use for release builds of the editor. It means "release (optimized) build with debugging/dev tools (`DEBUG_ENABLED`)".

The build matrix for desktop platforms is:

- Editor build: `tools=yes target=release_debug`
- Release template: `tools=no target=release`
- Debug template: `tools=no target=release_debug`

And then `target=debug` builds which are unoptimized and meant for engine developers (not part of the official builds matrix).

So for the Android editor we'll indeed want to use `target=release_debug`, i.e. the editor build is similar to a debug export template.

body:
The name is confusing, but this method was already there and is not really about the cursor itself, but rather what's underneath the cursor. It's actually about the selected TreeItem.

If I don't call "ensure_cursor_is_visible()" when unfolding, the TreeItem that was selected by the user might end up out of view. If the tree is big and requires scrolling both horizontally and vertically, it could end up scrolling the view completely to the right and down or anywhere else depending on the last operations the user did before collapsing everything. 

You normally want the item the user interacted with last to stay visible. 

I usually would agree though, I don't like enforcing things like that, but the goal of this method is to make the "Collapse All" logic the same everywhere across the editor so the UX stays consistent. 

The main use case for this method would be: 
RightClick a TreeItem, which selects it and open a context menu -> select in the menu "Collapse All" or "Extend All". 

Here's a quick example without ensure_cursor_is_visible():
![Ensure Cursor Visible False](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/52422077/82078846-d37f4d00-96af-11ea-9aed-f39eacb932ca.gif)

And here's with ensure_cursor_is_visible():
![Ensure Cursor Visible True](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/52422077/82079746-5a80f500-96b1-11ea-9c4c-0c482dcc844b.gif)

I'm open to changing it if needed, but if we do, maybe we should instead add a third boolean property like "skip_ensure_cursor_is_visible" so devs automatically know it's **supposed** to be the default behaviour?

What do you think?

Isn't it `blend -= b.blend_left / b.blend_time;`? I don't know, but I still think the blend weight calculation is wrong. It is doubted that the weighting can be justified when more than three blends are present.

To begin with, as I mentions in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/70241#issuecomment-1356843003, it is weird that blend value could exceed 1.0. I think it is most straight forward to iterate once for the calculation of blend weights before all blend animations go into process, and after that iterate again for process.
author: TokageItLab

body:
I've reversed the order in which the blends are processed so instead attempting to combine all the blends together like it was doing, I blend with the result of whatever blends are stacked up on top of each other.

For example, say anim1 is blending with anim2 and anim3 starts playing.

If we were 50% into the blend to anim2 and 25% into the blend of anim3, it would be like this:

anim1: blend of 1.0.  100% of animation is pose is used.
anim2: blend of 0.5.  50% of pose is used on top of everything before (in this case, just anim1)
anim3: blend of 0.25. 25% of the pose is used on top of everything before (the combined blend of anim 1 and 2).

The 1.0 - blend_left / blend_time is just to invert it to be fraction of the blend in instead of the blend out.  It's a little convoluted because the numbers/values were not meant to be processed in that order, but, fundamentally, I don't think the original logic could have worked.

Here, we're not getting 175% blending, as the values might imply, and we can't just weigh the blends before computing then combine them, because they need to blend *from the previous pose* not from the base pose, so we have to completely calculate the first anim, then blend with the combination of the first and second, then use that result to blend to the third and so on.  This should effectively allow unlimited blends.

See MRP in #69722 for reference. There is no blend there, but if you add a blend, I guess the problem will show up.

For example:
There are animations A, B, and C. A and B are now blended. In this case, the iterate order is A->B. If the method track in A changes animation A to C and the method callback mode is Immediate, then B will not be processed in the same frame; if that mode is Deferred, then it should be processed.

Although what is discarded and what is not discarded is determined by the iteration order, there is no way to confirm or set the iteration order as desired, so the user cannot determine what will happen.

> Also bis, where can I find the information about accepted standards per version ? I have only seen the c++03 somewhere, so I didn't even proposed the constexpr version ^^

We accept a subset of C++17 in the `master` branch, and full C++03 in stable branches like `3.2`. The subset in question is not formally written anywhere yet, but it boils down to "everything except `auto`, lambdas and `for` range loops" (more or less). This is done in the interest of writing more explicit code that's easier to review directly on GitHub.

Nice work! I've tested on a regular android phone and didn't spot any regression.

I've left some feedback in the code, mostly around button masks. I think the handling of button masks could be improved a little bit to make the code more flexible to changes in the future.

What I would suggest is to:
1. Have one place in java with constants directly reflecting the c++ ones (like you already did for mouse wheel in GodotInputHandler.java but with all the buttons)
2. Add some `static_assert` in the android display server to catch incompatibility in the future, something like:
```
// Constants need to be the same as in GodotInputHandler.java.
static_assert(BUTTON_MASK_LEFT == 1 << 0);
static_assert(BUTTON_MASK_RIGHT == 1 << 1);
etc.
```
3. Make sure button masks from android events are translated into the constants from 1. before they are mixed with Godot button masks and passed to the c++ side.

body:
Im suggesting that server tick _should_ be different. Im not talking about the frame rate, im talking about a virtual server tick.

As for i put validation, the whole point is to validate on the server to prevent cheating. The server should be authoritative. That is, nothing the client sends should be trusted and only the server shoukl tell other clients what the world state is. See: 

https://www.gabrielgambetta.com/client-server-game-architecture.html

This is almost always how modern multiplayer games are built in order to mitigate cheating.
author: jonbonazza

body:
@AndreaCatania thinking about this more, while an authoritative server model is _usually_ what you want, there are situations (e.g. in certain p2p games) where you don't really need and authoritative server model. I think that having the ability to be server authoritative is important though, as for things like player movement in an MMO, server authority is the  de factor implementation.

In super fast paced games like FPS, lockstep and authoritative servers are not ideal for some things though, so something like this would make more sense, possible couple with other networking concepts like lag compensation or anticheat software.

In the end, I think having the ability to work both ways is important.

I'm not sure what the best way to implement this would be tbh.

Sever authority is actually generally pretty game-specific for the most part and usually is handled via RPCs rather than replications of properties. The one big exception is movement, but perhaps that makes better sense to be implemented separately in a special `NetworkedKinematicBody` node or something that doesn't necessarily use this node.

body:
Yes, https://code.google.com/archive/p/bullet/issues/74 is definitely the cause for the weird behavior.

I understand you would like to make it work from Bullet directly, but in this case I think it's going to be easier to solve it on Godot side.

I've checked the ticket you linked before I've made my changes, and as much as the new formula might be more physically accurate in some edge cases, it makes it much harder to use in the simple case developers face for most games, which is being able to setup values for damping on a linear scale, with fixed time steps in physics.
All the details are well explained in #19182: with the new formula, if you want to fine-tune the damping values, you would need some values extremely close to 1 and this is cumbersome to set in the editor.

As for using `USE_OLD_DAMPING_METHOD`, I've tried it too but it doesn't work out of the box because of the damping values being clamped to 0..1 (we need higher values than 1 to be able to set the damping correctly with this method):
https://github.com/bulletphysics/bullet3/blob/b25d806b1460b2d70d7603311d260ec5ae4363cd/src/BulletDynamics/Dynamics/btRigidBody.cpp#L137-L141
author: pouleyKetchoupp

body:
Dump values higher than one breaks even your formula: `linear_vel *= MAX(0.0, 1.0 - delta_time * total_linear_damp);`

```
total_linear_damp = 1.5
delta_time = 1.0
1.0 - delta_time * total_linear_damp == -0.5
```
If you multiply the velocity by that value you invert the speed; so you need to rely on the function MAX to avoid this problem.

This is the reason why the damp can't be more than 1.

----

However, you may argue that `delta_time` is never 1; this doesn't matter since delta is not a value to scale the dumping, rather it's the time and the formula must work with any delta time span to be correct otherwise your formula will accumulate error overtime.

----

If you want to stop the body sooner you need a formula that scales the time, something like:
```
linear_vel *= (1.0 - delta_time * total_linear_damp) * damping_factor;
// OR
linear_vel *= 1.0 * time_scale - delta_time * time_scale * total_linear_damp;
```

Where `total_linear_damp` is always something between 0 and 1
author: AndreaCatania

body:
I'm applying the damping the exact same way it's done in Godot Physics:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/fcfffd729789cd80aa77056ca089697b52297d04/servers/physics_3d/body_3d_sw.cpp#L536-L547

It works in Godot Physics, and it works in my tests for this PR, with different values ranging from 0 to 100. As you mentioned, if the delta time was 1 the values would become negative, so they are clamped to 0 (full damping) by the MAX function. However, in most cases, delta time is a fixed value smaller than 1 so damping values over 1 make sense.

body:
So we didn't receive an answer for `Why the current Bullet damping is so weird? Is it correct and our expectations wrong or what?` so I propose to move this issue forward and fix it.

I think that the damping should always go between 0 and 1 (similarly on the Friction and Bounciness). Damping 1 mean that the body is completely stopped in 1 second. If the user would really need to stop the body sooner, it's likely that the damping is not the right tool to use, and it may want to add external forces.

So I would like to clamp the damping, on editor and on the Rigid Body, and use the bullet **legacy** equation. By clamping the damping, also Godot Physics will behave like Bullet Physics without further changes.
author: AndreaCatania

body:
Thanks, I agree with moving on with the bullet legacy equation. It will require a few changes within bullet code to compile so I'll make a PR on the bullet repo as well.

About the 0..1 clamping though, I don't see a good practical reason to do it. After the changes in the equation, Bullet and Godot will be working the exact same way, so there's no need to make further changes that would only cause a large range of use cases not to be supported anymore.

Using damping to stop a rigid body from moving faster than 1 second is a pretty common use case for games. Two examples that immediately come to my mind are:
- Physics-based character controllers have to stop quickly in order to avoid input/animation lag
- Joint stabilization for secondary animation often requires aggressive damping (see my example above)

body:
Yeah I was expecting we'd decide to do that, we can always look at the old version for reference.

In terms of maintenance, this is one of the most error prone areas actually. The logic in try_join must exactly match the logic in the renderer, otherwise you will get subtle rendering bugs as a result of joining items that shouldn't have been joined. In one of the other versions of the PR, I tried putting this all in the same uber function. However it does end up quite messy.

Although I've avoided the uber function approach here, I'm equally happy to go with either approach, there are pros and cons with both. The split version is easier to read and understand (especially for people unfamiliar with how it works). However the combined uber function may possibly be easier to maintain in the long run.

I think we can either change to uber function now, or leave as is and change with another PR if it proves to be a better approach. One other factor in favour of the split approach is that it might be easier initially in terms of dealing with ironing out major problems.

For the uber function to work it would probably either have to be littered with a lot of #ifdefs, or use templates, to ensure getting 2 different runtime versions of the function, versus lots of branching at runtime which would slow everything down unnecessarily.
author: lawnjelly

body:
Yes, pretty much. Essentially the problem is this: Any item that contains commands that are default (i.e. not handled by software transform and the batching renderer) should not be joined.

In order to work this out, it does a lookahead through the commands, which could potentially be very expensive. As such it makes sense to put a limit on this to some small number, which will catch nearly all cases which need joining, but not be overly expensive in the case of items with large numbers of commands.

There may be a far more efficient way of handling this. Ideally it would be nice in general to mark some extra data like this on the items themselves, and some dirty flags for when things change in the item. There's a lot of inefficiencies throughout to deal with the historical design.

In practice I don't think this will be a problem in 3.2 to do like this, but we could look at some better approaches in 4.0 where it might be possible to move some of this processing further up into the visual server.

author: madmiraal

body: The `btResult.m_closestHitFraction` returns the proportion of the move that will result in a collision, we need to find the proportion of the move that will **not** result in a collision: the safe distance. Furthermore, the `convexSweepTest` doesn't detect all collisions; so sometimes `btResult.m_closestHitFraction` is 1.0. A binary search is an effective means to find this proportion to any level of accuracy. With 8 steps (used in Godot physics too) the precision is 0.39% of the total move distance.

body:
Now `current_screen` gets set right before the popup position is changed, which might result in `current_window` being set, only for the window to be immediately moved to another screen.

Looking at the `DisplayServer` implementations, it seems that whenever a window's bounds are changed, the window gets notified of that through `Window::_rect_changed_callback` which should arguably be the place where the window's `current_screen` should actually be updated. This would make the value of `current_screen` more consistent and also allow `get_current_screen` to use the cached value instead of querying the `DisplayServer` every time.
author: opl-

body:
I tested the following cases:
 * current_screen set as in master (in popup) -> windows, like add node, will always beeing placed on main monitor
 * current_screen queried from current_screen in popup -> windows and popups open on the monitor of the active parent window
 * not setting current_screen in popup (only on resize) -> all windows and popups open on first screen. _rect_changed_callback does not provides desired effect, since the current screen is set and the position is updated based on the current_screen. Therefore setting it once in popup with the screen of the active parent window appears to be the only correct fix.
I want to emphasize this last point. You want your windows in your application on the same screen as the window you came from. The application should not just position it where it feels it is useful (i.e. the main screen)
author: HaSa1002

On Android, we don't build Vulkan source like we do on other platforms, and the error occurs when `vk_mem_alloc.h` is included in our source.

I'm going to fix it by using `GCC diagnostic ignored` when needed.
author: pouleyKetchoupp

body:
I don't think that's the right approach, we shouldn't have to disable specific warnings here, we want to ignore *all* warnings in thirdparty code as it's outside our jurisdiction. Otherwise when new warning types appear in vma, we'd have to blacklist each of them here. All thirdparty code in Godot should be built with warnings silenced.

Instead, it should be done as in `drivers/vulkan/SCsub`:
```
env_thirdparty = env.Clone()
env_thirdparty.disable_warnings()
vma_sources = [thirdparty_dir + "/vk_mem_alloc.cpp"]
env_thirdparty.add_source_files(env.drivers_sources, vma_sources)
```

And here you'd just include `vk_mem_alloc.h`.

body:
> On mobile anti-aliasing 4x is free

This isn't quite the case in my experience. I easily get a 30% performance drop by enabling 4x MSAA on a Samsung Galaxy Z Fold4 (which has a 8 Gen1+ SoC - a mid-2022 flagship), regardless of the resolution scale.

Anisotropic filtering is expected to be expensive on mobile due to limited memory bandwidth. Even 2x can have a significant impact on low-end devices. This is lessened when using bilinear filtering instead of trilinear filtering, but it comes at the cost of a harsh line between mipmaps that is especially noticeable in motion.

I don’t think that “defer” is the right word to use here. When you defer something, you cause that thing to happen later (this is how `call_deferred()` and `set_deferred()` use the word). Using `preload` causes the loading to happen _earlier_, not later. To make the example more clear, I would change it to:

```gdscript
# Loads the scene when the game reaches this line of code.
get_tree().change_scene_to(load("res://my_scene.tscn"))

# Loads the scene when this script is compiled. May not always work due to
# cyclic reference issues. If in doubt, use `load()`.
get_tree().change_scene_to(preload("res://my_scene.tscn"))
```

body: It's actually `final - increment`. So if `increment` is -1, it's `final + 1`, but if it's -13, it will be `final + 13`. (Or maybe not, actually it might be `final - (final - initial) % increment` or something like that... Which shows that equations are maybe not the best way to convey how the `range()` arguments are used.
